title: What hazard communication training does OSHA require, and what changed with the 2024 update?
description: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1200(h) hazard communication training, plus the 2024 HCS update and revised 2026 to 2028 compliance dates for employers, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) Hazard Communication Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1200(h), requires employers to give employees effective information and training on hazardous chemicals in their work area at initial assignment and whenever a new chemical hazard is introduced. The 2024 update took effect July 19, 2024. After a January 2026 amendment, employers must provide any additional training for newly identified hazards in substances by November 20, 2026 and in mixtures by May 19, 2028.
keyTakeaways: Hazard communication training is triggered by initial assignment and by the introduction of a new chemical hazard, not by a fixed annual cycle.

Paragraph (h)(3) sets four minimum training elements: detection methods, the hazards of chemicals in the work area, protective measures, and the details of the employer's program including labels and safety data sheets.
The 2024 final rule aligned the standard primarily with Revision 7 of the Globally Harmonized System and became effective July 19, 2024.
A final rule published January 15, 2026 revised the compliance dates: November 20, 2026 for employer training updates on substances and May 19, 2028 for mixtures.
Hazard communication was the second most cited federal OSHA standard in the preliminary fiscal year 2026 list, and the most cited in general industry.
jurisdiction: United States (federal, with state plan variations)
regulator: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), US Department of Labor
appliesTo: All employers whose employees are exposed to hazardous chemicals in their work area, including manufacturers that use chemicals in production, maintenance or cleaning
Chemical manufacturers, importers and distributors, which also classify hazards and prepare labels and safety data sheets
Employees who may be exposed to hazardous chemicals under normal conditions of use or in a foreseeable emergency

sections.heading: Who must provide hazard communication training?

blocks.text: Every employer with employees exposed to hazardous chemicals must train them. Paragraph (b)(1) of [29 CFR 1910.1200](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1910.1200) requires chemical manufacturers and importers to classify the hazards of chemicals they produce or import, and requires all employers to inform employees through a hazard communication program, labels, safety data sheets, and information and training.

The standard notes that employers who do not produce or import chemicals need only focus on the parts dealing with a workplace program and communicating information to workers. For a typical manufacturer, that means solvents, coolants, adhesives, coatings, welding consumables and cleaning agents all sit within scope, and many plants are also downstream users that relabel or transfer chemicals into secondary containers.

sections.heading: When must hazard communication training be given?

blocks.text: Training is required at initial assignment and whenever a new chemical hazard is introduced. Paragraph (h)(1) states that employers "shall provide employees with effective information and training on hazardous chemicals in their work area at the time of their initial assignment, and whenever a new chemical hazard the employees have not previously been trained about is introduced into their work area."

Training can be designed around categories of hazards, such as flammability or carcinogenicity, or around specific chemicals. Chemical-specific information must always remain available through labels and safety data sheets. A new product with the same hazard class as existing chemicals does not necessarily trigger retraining; a product that introduces a hazard class employees have not been trained on does.

sections.heading: What must hazard communication information and training cover?

blocks.text: The standard separates information from training. Under paragraph (h)(2), employees must be informed of the requirements of the section, the operations in their work area where hazardous chemicals are present, and the location and availability of the written program, the list of hazardous chemicals and the safety data sheets.
Under paragraph (h)(3), training must include at least:

items: Methods and observations that may be used to detect the presence or release of a hazardous chemical in the work area, such as employer monitoring, continuous monitoring devices, or the visual appearance or odor of chemicals when released.
The physical, health, simple asphyxiation, combustible dust and pyrophoric gas hazards, as well as hazards not otherwise classified, of the chemicals in the work area.
The measures employees can take to protect themselves, including specific procedures such as work practices, emergency procedures and personal protective equipment.

The details of the employer's program, including an explanation of labels on shipped containers, the workplace labeling system, and the safety data sheet, including the order of information and how employees can obtain and use it.

blocks.text: Paragraph (h) does not prescribe a training record format or retention period. Employers still need to show that training was effective, which in practice means being able to demonstrate what was covered, who attended, and that employees can read a label and find a safety data sheet.

sections.heading: What did the 2024 Hazard Communication Standard update change?

blocks.text: OSHA published a final rule on May 20, 2024 (89 FR 44356) that amended the standard primarily to align with Revision 7 of the Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (GHS). The [final rule](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/federalregister/2024-05-20) took effect July 19, 2024.

According to the rule's summary, the changes include revised criteria for classifying certain health and physical hazards, revised provisions for updating labels, new labeling provisions for small containers, new trade secret provisions, technical amendments to safety data sheet contents, and related changes to definitions. For employers who only use chemicals, the main effect is that suppliers will reclassify some products, which can introduce newly identified hazards onto labels and safety data sheets and therefore trigger training under (h)(1).

sections.heading: What are the current compliance dates for employers?

blocks.text: The compliance dates in paragraph (j) were revised by a final rule published January 15, 2026 (91 FR 1695), listed on [OSHA's Federal Register page for the notice](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/federalregister/2026-01-15). The current eCFR text sets the following dates. The first employer deadline falls on November 20, 2026, days after this page was published.

blocks.text: The employer duty is conditional: training is required "as necessary" for newly identified physical, health or other hazards. Employers should track revised safety data sheets from suppliers, compare the new classifications against what employees were trained on, and deliver targeted training where a new hazard class appears.

sections.heading: How can a manufacturer map hazard communication duties to evidence?

blocks.text: The most defensible approach treats the chemical inventory as the driver of training content. Each hazard class present in a work area becomes a learning outcome, and each supplier reclassification becomes a change event. sections.heading: How often is hazard communication cited?

blocks.text: Hazard communication is one of OSHA's most frequently cited standards. In the [preliminary fiscal year 2026 list](https://www.osha.gov/top10citedstandards) it ranks second across all industries and first among general industry standards. Maximum federal penalties for violations assessed after January 15, 2026 are published on [OSHA's penalties page](https://www.osha.gov/penalties).

Hazard communication training often overlaps with other chemical duties in a plant, such as [respiratory protection training](/regulations/osha-respiratory-protection-training-requirements) and the general expectations described in [OSHA training requirements](/regulations/osha-training-requirements). Transport of the same chemicals off site brings separate rules covered in [DOT hazmat employee training](/regulations/dot-hazmat-employee-training).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links each hazard class on a work area's chemical list to concepts and assessment points, so a supplier reclassification can be traced to the specific employees and outcomes it affects. That makes the conditional "as necessary" training duty in paragraph (j) something an organization can evidence item by item.

faqs.q: Does OSHA require annual hazard communication training?
faqs.a: No. Paragraph (h)(1) requires training at initial assignment and when a new chemical hazard is introduced into the work area. Many employers run annual refreshers by policy, and other standards such as respiratory protection do set annual cycles, but the Hazard Communication Standard itself does not.

faqs.q: Do all employees need retraining because of the 2024 update?
faqs.a: Not automatically. The employer duty in paragraph (j) is to provide additional training, as necessary, for newly identified hazards. If supplier reclassification adds a hazard employees were not trained on, targeted training is needed by November 20, 2026 for substances or May 19, 2028 for mixtures.

Yes. OSHA published a final rule on January 15, 2026 that revised paragraph (j). The current text sets May 19, 2026 and November 19, 2027 for chemical manufacturers, importers and distributors, and November 20, 2026 and May 19, 2028 for employer program, labeling and training updates.

faqs.q: Does hazard communication training have to be chemical by chemical?
faqs.a: No. The standard allows training designed around categories of hazards, such as flammability or carcinogenicity, or around specific chemicals. Chemical-specific details must always be available through labels and safety data sheets.
